# Gas turbine and jet engine (`gas_turbine_jet`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by steam_turbine, internal_combustion_engine, petroleum_refining, glider_aeroplane, heat_energy_conservation
- Core idea: A rotary compressor forces air continuously into a chamber where fuel burns at constant pressure; the hot gas drives a turbine on the same shaft as the compressor. What is left over is the output: shaft power, or in the jet engine a fast exhaust stream whose reaction pushes the aircraft. Useful output requires the turbine to supply more work than the compressor consumes. The balance depends on pressure ratio, inlet temperature and losses. Better compressors and heat-resistant alloys made compact aircraft engines practical.
- Pitfalls:
  - Overlooking the power needed by the compressor. Elling obtained a small net output in 1903, decades before useful turbojets
  - Thinking a jet pushes against the air behind it; thrust is the reaction to the gas thrown backward
  - Crediting only Whittle or only von Ohain; both worked independently
  - Ordinary steel in the turbine, which creeps and fails at red heat
- History: china: c. 12th c. – hot-air zoetrope lanterns turned by rising gas, a toy turbine; europe: 1791 – John Barber's gas turbine patent; 1903 Ægidius Elling's turbine gives the first net power (Norway); 1930 Frank Whittle's turbojet patent, engine run April 1937, flight 15 May 1941; 1937 Hans von Ohain's engine runs, first jet flight in the Heinkel He 178 on 27 August 1939; 1939 Brown Boveri gas-turbine power station at Neuchâtel
- Read:
  - Edward W. Constant II, The Origins of the Turbojet Revolution (1980)
  - John Golley, Whittle: The True Story (1987)
